titleStmt.title: Sustainable multiprocessor scheduling of sporadic task systems

analytic.title: Sustainable multiprocessor scheduling of sporadic task systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: A scheduling policy or a schedulability test is defined to be sustainable with respect to a particular workload model if any task system represented in that model that is determined to be schedulable remains so if it behaves better than mandated by its specifications. We investigate the sustainability properties of global scheduling algorithms when applied to systems represented using the sporadic task model. We show that Fixed-Priority (FP) scheduling of sporadic task sets is sustainable under a variety of scheduling parameter relaxations, including decreased execution requirements, later arrivals, and deadline relaxations. It follows that all sufficient tests of global FP schedulability are sustainable for sporadic task systems. We show that the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) and Earliest-Deadline with Zero Laxity scheduling policies are sustainable with respect to decreased execution requirements and later arrivals. We also introduce a notion of self-sustainability, and show that many widely-used EDF schedulability tests are not selfsustainable but one is.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Analytical methods of validating system timing constraints rely on workload models that are typically specified in terms of "worst-case" parameters. Consider, for instance, the sporadic task model [13,5]. In this model, a sporadic task τ i is characterized by three parameters C i , D i , and T i . Such a task generates a potentially infinite sequence of jobs: C i denotes the maximum execution requirement of each job, T i the minimum inter-arrival separation between successive jobs, and D i the maximum amount of time that may elapse between a job's arrival and the completion of its execution. Actual behavior during run-time often falls short of these extremes. Jobs may execute for less than C i time units, arrive more than T i time units apart, and have actual deadlines that are more than D i time units after their arrival times. So, for such analyses to be useful in practical applications it is essential that the nominal "worst-case" parameters represent the true worst case.

Several efforts have been made to express this important property. Ha and Liu [12,11] showed that certain classes of scheduling policies are "predictable" in the sense that if a collection of jobs is scheduled to meet all deadlines the same is also true if some of the job execution times are shortened, and so it is valid for an analysis to limit consideration to situations in which all tasks use their maximum execution times. Mok and Poon [14] called a scheduling algorithm for periodic task systems "robust" if schedulability is preserved under increases in task periods as well as decreases in task execution times. Most recently, Burns and Baruah [4,7] introduced the term "sustainability", and applied it to invariance of analytically derived schedulability guarantees under a broader range of workload variations, including: (i) decreased execution requirements; (ii) larger periods; (iii) smaller release-time jitter; and (iv) larger relative deadlines.

In this paper we consider the sustainability of several global scheduling algorithms when scheduling sporadic task systems on a set of identical multiprocessors. After reviewing the definitions, we will show that global fixed priority (FP) scheduling is fully sustainable, and that Earliest Deadline First (EDF) and earliest-deadline until zero laxity (EDZL) is sustainable with respect to some forms of parameter relaxation. We then argue that for practical purposes a schedulability test should be sustainable in a stronger sense, which we call self-sustainability. We review several known schedulability tests for global EDF, showing that some are self-sustainable and some are not.

div.head: Model and definitions
div.p: In real-time scheduling theory, a real-time system is typically specified using some formal workload model. In many of these models, a job is defined to be the basic unit of work that needs to be executed. In the arbitrary job sets model (used in this paper in, for example, Observation 4) a workload is specified as an explicit collection of individual jobs. In more sophisticated models (such as the periodic and sporadic task models), the workload is specified as a finite collection of recurrent tasks, each of which generates a potentially infinite number of jobs. The primary focus of this research is on workloads that are specified according to the sporadic task model and a natural generalization which we call the relaxed sporadic task model; these models are discussed in greater detail in Section 2.1.

Each real-time system has an associated scheduling policy that is responsible for determining, at run time, which job[s] should execute at each instant in time. Important associated concepts are discussed in Section 2.2 below, along with descriptions of the major scheduling policies -EDF, FP, and EDZL -considered in this paper.

The concept of sustainability, which is the major focus of this paper, is defined with respect to specific scheduling policies when applied to specific workload models. Our focus is on the sustainability of global scheduling policies, for the sporadic and relaxed sporadic workload models. Sustainability is discussed further in Section 2.3 below.

div.head: Sporadic Tasks
div.p: As stated in Section 1 above, a sporadic task τ i = (C i , D i , T i ) is characterized by a worst-case execution requirement C i , a (relative) deadline D i , and a period or minimum inter-arrival separation parameter T i . Such a sporadic task generates a potentially infinite sequence of jobs, with successive job-arrivals separated by at least T i time units. Each job has a worst-case execution requirement equal to C i and a deadline that occurs D i time units after its arrival time. We refer to the interval, of size D i , between such a job's arrival instant and deadline as its scheduling window. We assume a fully preemptive execution model: any executing job may be interrupted at any instant in time, and its execution resumed later with no cost or penalty. A sporadic task system is comprised of a finite number of such sporadic tasks. It is evident from the definition of sporadic tasks, and of sporadic task systems, that any given system may generate infinitely many different collections of jobs.
In the remainder of this paper, we will let τ denote a system of n sporadic tasks:
div.formula: τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . τ n }, with τ i = (C i , D i , T i ) for all i, 1 ≤ i ≤ n.

div.head: Scheduling policies and schedulability tests
div.p: As stated above, a scheduling policy in a real-time system determines, at each instant during run-time, which job[s] should be executed. A workload is said to be schedulable by a given scheduling policy if the policy guarantees to meet all deadlines for the workload. For a given schedul-ing policy and a particular workload model, a schedulability test accepts as input the specifications of a workload specified in that model and determines whether the workload is schedulable by that scheduling policy.

As is evident from its definition, a sporadic task system may generate infinitely many different collections of jobs during different executions. A schedulability test for a given scheduling policy and the sporadic workload model must therefore guarantee that the scheduling policy will meet all deadlines in each and every one of these different collections of jobs. More precisely, let A denote a scheduling policy. A sporadic task system is said to be A-schedulable upon a specified platform if A meets all deadlines when scheduling each of the potentially infinite different collections of jobs that could be generated by the sporadic task system, upon the specified platform. An A-schedulability test accepts as input the specifications of a sporadic task system and a multiprocessor platform, and determines whether the task system is A-schedulable. An A-schedulability test is said to be exact if it identifies all A-schedulable systems, and sufficient if it identifies only some A-schedulable systems.

Global EDF scheduling. Global EDF scheduling is the preemptive scheduling policy for multiprocessor systems that ensures that jobs with earlier deadlines are always executed ahead of jobs with later deadlines. That is, there is a single global queue of uncompleted jobs, and at all times the set of jobs that is executing is a set of jobs with the earliest deadlines. No processors are ever idled while there are jobs to execute. The cost of preempting a job on one processor and resuming it on a different processor is assumed to be comparable to the cost of resuming the job on the same processor later. For simplicity of explanation, the costs of preemption and migration are not explicitly accounted for in the following analyses. However, those costs can be accounted for by adding a constant to the worst-case execution time of each task, since a preemption can only occur with global EDF scheduling in response to a new job arrival and a migration can only occur in response to a job completion.

EDF scheduling has long been known to be optimal for sporadic task systems on single-processor systems, in the sense that if there exists a schedule that meets all deadlines EDF scheduling will find such a schedule. This optimality does not extend to multiprocessor systems. Indeed, Fisher [10] has shown that no on-line algorithm for scheduling sporadic task systems can be optimal in this sense.

Global fixed-priority scheduling. Fixed-priority (FP) scheduling policies have been widely studied for workload models that represent the workload as a finite collection of recurrent tasks. In these scheduling policies, a distinct priority must be assigned to each recurrent task. Global FP scheduling is a preemptive scheduling policy much like global EDF, except that at all times the set of jobs that is executing is a set of jobs generated by tasks with the greatest priorities. With respect to the sporadic sporadic workload model, a common FP scheduling policy is deadlinemonotonic (DM), in which priorities are assigned to tasks depending on the value of their relative deadline parameters (with smaller deadlines corresponding to greater priority).
Global EDZL scheduling. Earliest Deadline until Zero Laxity (EDZL) is another widely-studied global scheduling policy [9,1,8]. We discuss this policy further in Section 4.

div.head: Sustainability
div.p: It would be unsafe to rely upon any schedulability test for practical purposes if a task system that is deemed schedulable by the test may fail to meet all deadlines if the system behaves better at run time than the specifications. The notion of sustainability formalizes this expectation: intuitively, sustainability requires that schedulability be preserved in situations in which it should be "easier" to ensure schedulability. As explained in [4,7], sustainability of schedulability guarantees under relaxations of timing parameters is a very basic and fundamental requirement in the engineering or hard-real-time systems, since it is only very rarely that a system can be characterized exactly (rather than by upper bounds) at system design time.

Sustainability is defined in [4,7] as a property of a scheduling policy (and its associated schedulability tests). But what constitutes "better" than worst-case behavior of a system is intimately linked to the manner in which the system is specified. Consider, for instance, systems specified according to the arbitrary job sets model. Such a system can reasonably be said to behave better than its specifications if some jobs execute for less than their worst-case execution time specifications, and/ or have actual deadlines later than their specified deadlines. However, some (not all) jobs arriving later than specified would not be considered to constitute better behavior, since this would tend to cause overload at a later point in time. For systems that are specified according to the sporadic tasks model, decreased execution times and larger relative deadlines continue to constitute better behavior than specified; in addition, jobs of a task arriving more than the minimum inter-arrival separation apart could also reasonably be said to be behaving better than specified.

Given this strong link between the notion of better behavior and the workload model, we believe that sustainability is appropriately defined with respect to specific workload models. In this paper, the workload model considered is the sporadic task model. As we have seen, any given sporadic task system may generate infinitely many different job sets, and such a task system is said to be schedulable by a particular scheduling policy only if the scheduling policy is able to successfully schedule all these job sets. Sustainability of scheduling policies and schedulability tests for sporadic task systems must hence also take into consideration all the different job sets that may be generated by a given task system. With respect to the sporadic workload model, the definition of sustainability may be stated as follows:

Definition 1 (Sustainable scheduling policy) Let A denote a scheduling policy. Let τ denote any sporadic task system that is A-schedulable. Let J denote a collection of jobs generated by τ . Scheduling policy A is said to be sus-

div.head: tainable if and only if A meets all deadlines when scheduling any collection of jobs obtained from J by changing the parameters of one or more individual jobs in any, some, or all of the following ways: (i) decreased execution requirements; (ii) larger relative deadlines; and (iii) later arrival times with the restriction that successive jobs of any task τ i ∈ τ arrive at least T i time units apart.
div.p: If A is a sustainable scheduling policy, then every sufficient A-schedulability test possesses the desired property that any sporadic task system deemed A-schedulable will remain A-schedulable if it behaves better than specified. For scheduling policies that are not sustainable, though, not every schedulability test possesses this desirable property. Those that do are called sustainable schedulability tests: Definition 2 (Sustainable schedulability test) Let A denote a scheduling policy, and F an A-schedulability test for sporadic task systems. Let τ denote any sporadic task system deemed to be A-schedulable by F . Let J denote a collection of jobs generated by τ . F is said to be a sustainable schedulability test if and only if scheduling policy A meets all deadlines when scheduling any collection of jobs obtained from J by changing the parameters of one or more individual jobs in any, some, or all of the following ways: (i) decreased execution requirements; (ii) larger relative deadlines; and (iii) later arrival times with the restriction that successive jobs of any task τ i ∈ τ arrive at least T i time units apart.

We would like to stress that declaring a scheduling policy or a schedulability test for sporadic task systems to be sustainable represents a stronger claim than simply that a task system deemed schedulable would remain schedulable with better parameters (e.g., with a larger period or relative deadline, or a smaller execution requirement). In addition, sustainability demands that a system deemed schedulable continue to meet all deadlines even if the parameter changes are occurring on line during run-time. We also permit that the parameters change back and forth, on a job-to-job basis, arbitrarily many times. The only restriction we will place on such parameter-changing is that each generated job have exactly one arrival time, execution requirement, and deadline during its lifetime.

A scheduling policy or schedulability test for sporadic task systems may be sustainable with respect to some, but not all three, job parameters. A scheduling policy or a schedulability test for sporadic task systems is said to be sustainable if it is sustainable with respect to all three parameters.

3 Sustainability of global EDF and FP It was shown in [4,7] that both EDF and FP scheduling of sporadic task systems are sustainable under all three forms of scheduling parameter relaxations mentioned in Definition 1, for single processor systems. In this section we will explore the degree to which this sustainability generalizes to multiprocessor systems.

div.head: Decreased execution time
div.p: Suppose that the specified WCET of a job is C. There are at least two ways in which this job may behave better than its specifications with respect to execution times. One, it may become known at (or prior to) the instant that the job arrives, that its WCET is actually C for some C < C. And two, the actual execution time C of the job is likely to be strictly less than C as well; we assume that the value of C is not known before the job completes, but can only become known by executing the job to completion. Since the EDF and FP scheduling policies do not use the WCET of a job in making scheduling decisions, the first kind of better behavior -knowing, prior to a job's arrival, a better estimate of its WCET -does not impact the schedule generated 1 . We now show that both the EDF and FP scheduling policies are sustainable with respect to decreases in the actual execution times of jobs.

Observation 1 Both the global EDF and FP scheduling policies are sustainable with respect to decreased execution requirements, for any collection of jobs, including any set of jobs that may be generated by a set of sporadic tasks. (It therefore follows that the global EDF and FP scheduling of sporadic task systems are sustainable with respect to decreased execution requirements.) Proof: Ha and Liu [12,11] showed that schedulability is "predictable", and therefore sustainable, under shortening of execution times for a large class of preemptive migrateable multiprocessor scheduling policies, including global EDF and FP.

div.head: Later arrival times
div.p: Observation 2 Any scheduling policy, including global EDF and FP, is sustainable for sporadic task systems with 1 We will see in Section 4 that such is not the case with the EDZL scheduling policy, which does use WCET to make scheduling decisions.

div.head: respect to later arrival times.
div.p: Proof: Let τ denote a sporadic task system, and J a collection of jobs generated by τ . Let J denote any collection of jobs obtained from J by increasing the arrival times of one or more individual jobs with the restriction that successive jobs of any task τ i ∈ τ arrive at least T i time units apart. The collection J of jobs could also have been generated by τ . The observation follows, as a consequence.

div.head: Larger relative deadlines
div.p: Changes in job deadlines do not affect the schedule for global FP scheduling policies. Observation 3 trivially follows:
Observation 3 Global FP scheduling policies are sustainable for sporadic task systems with respect to larger relative deadlines.

However, sustainability with respect to deadline relaxation is not quite so straightforward with regards to EDF. In discussing deadline relaxations, there is some ambiguity regarding the implementation of global EDF. Specifically, the sustainability property may be expected to depend on whether EDF will prioritize jobs during run-time based on the actual deadlines of jobs, or their specified deadlines (which can be obtained for each job by adding its specified relative deadline parameter to its actual arrival time). If the specified deadlines are used to determine job priorities, then global EDF is trivially sustainable for the same reason that FP scheduling policies are: changes to actual job deadlines do not affect the schedule. However, if actual job deadlines are used in determining job priorities, then it is not obvious that EDF is sustainable with respect to deadline relaxation. Indeed, Observation 4 below illustrates that global EDF is not sustainable with respect to deadline relaxation, for the model in which the workload is specified as an arbitrary collection of jobs. (This is in contrast to the uniprocessor case, where EDF has been shown [4,Theorem 4] to be sustainable with respect to deadline relaxation for this workload model.)

div.head: Observation 4
div.p: The global EDF scheduling policy is not sustainable with respect to later deadlines for the arbitrary job sets model.

Proof: Let jobs J 1 and J 2 have execution time 1 and relative deadline 2.01, and let job J 3 have execution time 2 and relative deadline 2.00. Assume all three jobs are released at the same time, and assume there are two processors. Since J 3 has the earliest deadline, it will start executing on one processor immediately, while J 1 and J 2 run on the other processor, sequentially. All three jobs will complete within their deadlines, by time 2. Now, suppose the deadline of jobs J 3 is relaxed slightly, to 2.02. This will cause jobs J 1 and J 2 to execute first, causing completion of job J 3 to be delayed to time 3, missing its deadline.

From the above example, it seems that for this particular workload model (arbitrary collections of jobs) global EDF might be an example of a situation where a conservative sufficient schedulability test that is sustainable is preferable to an exact one, because any exact test would be unsustainable. We do not yet know whether the same holds with regards to the sporadic task system model, or whether EDF is in fact sustainable with respect to deadline relaxation for sporadic task systems. In the absence of definitive knowledge of its sustainability, we would recommend that for scheduling sporadic task systems, the use of global EDF only be used in restricted circumstances:
1. It is safe to use EDF for scheduling systems for which it is a priori known that deadline relaxations cannot occur.
2. Otherwise, it is safe to use EDF if it can be implemented such that specified, rather than actual, job deadlines are used in determining job priority.

div.head: Sustainability of global EDZL
div.p: Earliest Deadline (until) Zero Laxity (EDZL) is another widely-studied global scheduling policy [9,1,8]. For any job J let e(J) denote its WCET and d(J) its (absolute, not relative) deadline. For any schedule S and any time-instant t, let alloc(S, J, t) denote the amount of execution J has received in schedule S over [0, t). Let remain(S, J, t) denote its remaining execution requirement in schedule S at time t: remain(S, J, t) def = e(J)alloc(S, J, t). The laxity of J in schedule S at time t is defined as follows:
div.formula: laxity(S, J, t) def = d(J) -t -remain(S, J, t) .
div.p: The EDZL scheduling policy prioritizes jobs based on both deadlines and laxity: jobs with zero laxity are assigned greatest priority (ties broken arbitrarily), while the relative priorities of jobs that have laxity greater than zero are as with EDF.

EDZL is known to strictly dominate EDF with respect to all commonly-used workload models, in the sense that all EDF-schedulable systems are also EDZL-schedulable, whereas there are EDZL-schedulable systems that EDF fails to schedule. Also, EDZL exhibits good preemption properties that are comparable to those of EDF: an EDZL schedule does not contain any additional preemptions over and above what an EDF schedule does unless the EDF schedule would miss a deadline, and in no case does an EDZL schedule have more than one additional preemption per job. In this section, we study the sustainability properties of EDZL scheduling for both the arbitrary job-sets model and the sporadic tasks model. We show that EDZL is sustainable with respect to later arrivals (Section 4.1), and with respect to decreased execution requirements under two different interpretations of how EDZL would adapt its behavior to such decreases (Section 4.2). We discuss sustainability of EDZL with respect to relaxed deadlines in Section 4.3.

div.head: Later arrival times
div.p: Observation 5 EDZL is sustainable for sporadic task systems with respect to later arrival times.

Proof: This follows for the same reason, presented in the proof of Observation 2, that EDF and FP scheduling policies are sustainable for later arrival times. Let τ denote a sporadic task system, and J a collection of jobs generated by τ . Let J denote any collection of jobs obtained from J by increasing the arrival times of one or more individual jobs with the restriction that successive jobs of any task τ i ∈ τ arrive at least T i time units apart. The collection J of jobs could also have been generated by τ .

div.head: Decreased execution times
div.p: We now turn our attention to studying the sustainability properties of EDZL with respect to decreased execution times. As was the case with deadline relaxation and EDF, the impact of execution-time decreases on EDZL scheduling depends upon how EDZL uses execution-times in computing laxities and thereby determining job priorities. Suppose that a job is generated by sporadic task τ i = (C i , D i , T i ) during run-time, but at the instant that it is generated, it becomes known that its actual execution time will be no more than some C i < C i . Two different implementations of EDZL are possible, depending on whether the specified worst-case execution time C i or the "better" worst-case execution time C i is used to compute laxity 2 .

If the specified value -C i -is used, then the sustainability property we seek is essentially the same as the predictability property of Ha and Liu [12,11]. However, the results in [12,11] only apply to scheduling policies that do not change the priorities assigned to individual jobs; since the priority of a job may change in EDZL scheduling if it becomes a zero-laxity job, these results do not imply predictability of EDZL. We show below (Lemma 1) that EDZL is sustainable with regard to decreased execution times under both interpretations at to how laxities are computed: that the execution times used in computing laxities are the ones provided in the system specifications, or less pessimistic values that become known upon job arrival.

Predictability properties of EDZL with respect to decreases in execution time have previously been shown to hold in [15], both when exact execution times are known at time of job arrival (and are used to compute laxities), and when the actual execution time of a job is not known until it finishes (so that its laxity must be computed based on specified WCET). Our sustainability properties could in principle be derived from these results, however we have chosen to provide a proof from first principles below.

div.head: Lemma 1
div.p: The EDZL scheduling policy is sustainable for both arbitrary collections of jobs and for sporadic task systems with respect to decreased execution requirements.

Proof: We will prove a stronger result. Let J denote a collection of jobs that is EDZL-schedulable on m processors, and J a collection of jobs obtained from J by decreasing some of the execution requirements. For each J ∈ J , let J ∈ J denote the job obtained in this manner from J. We will show that for all t ≥ 0, ∀J : J ∈ J : remain(S , J , t) ≤ remain(S, J, t) , (1) where S and S denote the EDZL schedules for J and J respectively. The lemma will follow, since by assumption J is EDZL-schedulable and hence remain(S, J, d(J)) = 0 for all J ∈ J .

(Observe that the computation of remain(S, J, t) depends on which interpretation of decreased execution times is being considered. That is, if the specified WCET's are used then remain(S, J, t) is the difference between the specified WCET C i of the task τ i that generated J and the amount alloc(S, J, t) of execution it has received thus far; if a more accurate estimate C i becomes available at jobrelease time and is used, then remain(S, J, t) is equal to C ialloc(S, J, t). The arguments below -and hence, Inequality 1 -remain valid regardless of which interpretation is used.) Suppose that the statement above is false. That is, there exists some pair of job sets J and J that differ only as specified, but for which some job has greater remaining execution requirement in J than in J at some time-instant t.
Observe that Inequality 1 is true at t = 0, since
• alloc(S , J , 0) = alloc(S, J, 0) = 0, for all J;
• d(J ) = d(J) for all J; and
• e(J ) = e(J) if specified WCET's are used in computing laxities, while e(J ) ≤ e(J) if a less pessimistic estimate of J 's WCET becomes available and is used.
Consider the first time-instant t 1 at which Inequality 1 is false, and suppose that it is false for some job J 1 : remain(S , J 1 , t 1 ) > remain(S, J 1 , t 1 ) .

Since Inequality 1 is true at t 1 -1 but is false at t 1 , it must be the case that J 1 executes in S, whereas J 1 does not execute in S , over the time-interval [t 1 -1, t 1 ) (as before, we are assuming a discrete model of time). Since Inequality 1 is true at t 1 -1 and d(J) = d(J ) for all jobs J, it must be the case that laxity(S , J , t 1 -1) ≥ laxity(S, J, t 1 -1)

for all jobs J. Directly from this observation, it follows that 1. If any job J is active at time-instant t 1 -1 in S then J is also active at this instant in S; and 2. if any job J has zero laxity at time-instant t 1 -1 in S then J also has zero laxity at this instant in S.

Since for all jobs that are active at t 1 -1 in J , their corresponding jobs are also active in J , the reason why J 1 executes over [t 1 -1, t 1 ) in S but J 1 does not execute over this interval in S is because J 1 has greater priority in S than J 1 does in S at time-instant t 1 -1. Now from the requirement that J is EDZL-schedulable, it follows that there are at most m zero-laxity jobs in S at time-instant t 1 -1. From Inequality 3 above, it follows that there are at most m zero-laxity jobs in S at time-instant t 1 -1. Since the deadlines of corresponding jobs are exactly the same in both J and J , it must be the case that 1. J 1 is a zero-laxity job in S at time-instant t 1 -1; and 2. J 1 is not a zero-laxity job in S at time-instant t 1 -1.
From the latter fact, we conclude that remain(S , J 1 , t 1 -1) < d(J 1 ) -(t 1 -1), which, under our discrete model of time, in turn implies that remain(S , J 1 , t 1 ) ≤ d(J 1 )t 1 .
On the other hand, since J is a zero-laxity job in S at t 1 -1, it remains a zero-laxity job at all subsequent timeinstants until its deadline. Hence
Since d(J 1 ) = d(J 1 ), we arrive at a contradiction to the assumption that remain(S , J 1 , t 1 ) > remain(S, J 1 , t 1 ), and the lemma is proved.

div.head: Larger relative deadlines
div.p: As was the case with global EDF, we do not yet know whether EDZL is sustainable with respect to deadline relaxation for sporadic task systems. In the absence of definitive knowledge of its sustainability, we would recommend that the use of EDZL be used in restricted circumstances:
1. It is safe to use EDZL for scheduling systems for which it is a priori known that deadline relaxations cannot occur.

2. Otherwise, it is safe to use EDZL if it can be implemented such that specified, rather than actual, job deadlines are used in determining both aspects of job priorities -the deadline and the laxity.

div.head: Combinations of relaxations
div.p: We have shown that global FP, EDF and EDZL scheduling of sporadic task systems is sustainable under several different kinds of parameter relaxation. The following lemma tells us that they are also sustainable under any combination of these kinds of relaxations.

div.head: Lemma 2 If a scheduling policy is sustainable under individual kinds of parameter relaxations, for sporadic task systems, then it is sustainable under the same relaxations in any combination.
div.p: Proof: Suppose the contrary. That is, suppose a scheduling policy is sustainable under each of several kinds of parameter relaxations individually, but not in combination.
There must then be a task systems τ , a job set J generated by τ , and another job set J such that 1. J can be obtained from J by a finite sequence of some combination of job parameter relaxations.
2. J is scheduled to meet all deadlines.
3. J is scheduled and fails to meet at least one deadline.

Since there are a finite number of jobs in J , there are a finite number of individual job scheduling parameter relaxations, forming a continuum of job sets between J and J , each pair of which differs by only one job parameter relaxation. It follows that for one of these pairs, the first job set is schedulable and the second job set is not. That pair of job sets differs by only one kind of scheduling parameter relaxation. This is a contradiction of the hypothesis.

Lemma 2 says that we can safely focus on just one kind of sustainability at a time, and rely that if a system is sustainable under each kind of relaxation separately, it will also be sustainable under any combination.

div.head: Self-sustainable schedulability tests
div.p: Sustainability of schedulability tests, as defined in Definition 2, provides a guarantee that if a task system is deemed schedulable by the test, it will not fail to meet all deadlines if the system behaves better at run time than the specifications. We now define a different kind of sustainability property for schedulability tests: Definition 3 (self-sustainability) A schedulability test is self-sustainable if all task systems with "better" (less constraining) parameters than a task system deemed schedulable by the test are also be deemed schedulable by the test.

We call this form of sustainability self-sustainability to emphasize the difference between this and the preceding definition of sustainability: the system is not only required to remain schedulable under various parameter relaxations, but it is required to be verifiably schedulable by the same test.

One motivation for this notion of self-sustainability arises from the needs of the incremental, interactive design process that is typically used in the design of real-time systems and in the evolutionary development of fielded systems. Ideally, such a design process allows for interactive exploration of the space of possible designs; this is greatly facilitated if changes that are viewed as relaxations of constraints actually result in making feasible larger regions of the design space. If a self-sustainable schedulability test is used, then relaxing timing constraints (e.g, increasing relative deadlines or periods, or decreasing worst-case execution times) will not render schedulable sub-systems unschedulable (or the practical equivalent: unverifiable). For example, suppose one were designing a composite system comprised of several subsystems, and had reached a point where most subsystems are deemed schedulable by the schedulability test. One could safely consider relaxing the task parameters of the schedulable subsystems in order to search for neighboring points in the design state space in which the currently unschedulable sub-systems may also be deemed schedulable, without needing to worry that the currently schedulable sub-systems would unexpectedly be deemed unschedulable.

div.head: Global-EDF schedulability tests that are not self-sustainable
div.p: We will now show that several well-known sufficient tests for global EDF schedulability are not self-sustainable; in Section 6.2, we will show that one other is selfsustainable. Self-sustainability of the remaining tests has not yet been studied.

A sufficient EDF-schedulability test for constrained deadline sporadic task systems3 is derived in [6] in the following manner. Define the interference of τ i on some job of τ k to be the duration within the job of τ k 's scheduling window during which τ i is executing but τ k is not. Define N i,k to be the largest number of jobs of τ i that may lie entirely within one job of τ k :

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Sustainable scheduling policies ensure that a system whose schedulability has been successfully validated will meet all its deadlines at run-time even if its operating parameters change for the better during system run-time. We believe that such sustainability is a critical requirement in the engineering of safety-critical real-time systems. Accordingly, we have subjected the multiprocessor global scheduling of sporadic task systems to a thorough analysis from the perspective of sustainability. We have shown that global FP scheduling is sustainable under decreased execution times, increased inter-arrival times, and increased deadlines for this workload model, and that global EDF and EDZL scheduling are sustainable under decreased execution times and increased inter-arrival times.
Along the way, we have clarified the relationship between sustainability, scheduling policy, and workload model.

We have also introduced a new, stronger notion of sustainability for schedulability tests, called self-sustainability. We have provided examples from previously known schedulability tests for global EDF of tests that are not selfsustainable, and a test that is self-sustainable.

This work has also raised some new questions that remain to be answered. Among those questions are whether the remaining known sufficient schedulability tests for global EDF are self-sustainable, and whether they can be extended to cover the relaxed sporadic task model. Another interesting question is whether there are examples of desirable scheduling policies that are not sustainable, but for which there exist self-sustainable tests.
